The structure of the malaria parasite HAD1 sugar phosphatase in complex with multiple substrates reveals that cap-domain closure facilitates diverse sugar phosphate recognition and catalysis.
the cap domain of HAD enzymes undergoes a large structural change upon substrate binding, which facilitates substrate recognition and catalytic function within this large superfamily of enzymes.
the cap domain of C2-type HAD enzymes undergoes a conformational change from open to closed upon substrate binding that facilitates substrate recognition and catalytic activity.

the molecular mechanism of a sugar phosphatases in malaria parasites.
understanding the structural determinants of substrate specificity in the HAD super-family of enzymes.
the structure and function of enzymes that are involved in the metabolism of sugars.

the cap movement is the key structural feature that enables substrate binding and specificity within the HADs superfamily.

cap movement within C2 HAD superfamily members enables diverse substrate recognition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the structural determinants of substrate recognition and catalytic activity within a large super-family of enzymes have been determined.
the cap domain of PfHAD is flexible in the cap-open state, and becomes ordered and makes specific interactions with substrate in the cap-closed state.
the structural basis for catalysis in a large superfamily is defined by the substrate-binding regions of the cap domain.

the HADs are an extremely diverse family of enzymes that share a common fold and mechanism.
